findings.claim: the shield protected not only the carrier but the left side of the man standing to his right
findings.truth: A hoplite carried the shield on his left arm, protecting himself and the man standing to his left.
findings.evidence: Fetched Wikipedia, Hoplite: shield placement and phalanx drift section.

findings.claim: Two prescribed visual sources illuminate hoplite warfare directly.
findings.truth: The Corinthian-type helmet is prescribed, but the Mycenaean Warrior Vase is not in the J199/23 prescribed visual/material source list.
findings.evidence: OCR J199 specification, War and Warfare prescribed visual/material sources, p. 27.

findings.claim: hoplon, the name for the large round shield
findings.truth: Use either the conventional school term throughout, or revise all linked teaching and checks to distinguish hoplon (equipment) from aspis (shield). The correction would ripple through the lesson’s questions, flashcards and glossary.
findings.evidence: Fetched Wikipedia, Hoplite and Ancient Greek warfare: hoplon refers to equipment; the shield is aspis.
findings.ruling: Conventional hoplon kept; one sentence adds the aspis distinction.

findings.claim: a child deemed weak or deformed was not raised but exposed on the slopes of Mount Apothetas
findings.truth: This is a claim in the much later Plutarch. No contemporary source or archaeological evidence confirms it as standard Spartan practice.
findings.evidence: Fetched Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 16; fetched Wikipedia, Sparta, Birth and death section.

findings.claim: was a period in which promising young men were sent into the countryside, armed with only a dagger, to live off the land and kill helots
findings.truth: Either present Plutarch’s account explicitly as one later source and explain that the krypteia’s purpose is disputed, or retain the current simplified account. This affects the definition, prose, practice material, flashcards and glossary, so it is not a surgical correction.
findings.evidence: Fetched Wikipedia, Crypteia and Agoge: Plato, Aristotle and Plutarch give different accounts; modern interpretations differ.
findings.ruling: One sentence attributes the account to Plutarch and flags the scholarly dispute; simplified account kept.

findings.claim: For essay questions on why Marathon was significant
findings.truth: Either retain Marathon as clearly labelled contextual enrichment, or replace the lesson with prescribed content. J199/23 names Thermopylae and Salamis as the Greek key battles, while also allowing wider sources for context; changing this lesson would ripple throughout its fields.
findings.evidence: OCR J199 specification, War and Warfare content, pp. 26–29.
findings.ruling: Lesson labelled as context; prescribed battles named. Not deleted.

findings.claim: Salamis made it impossible for Xerxes to supply or reinforce his army, so later land battles could not have ended Greek resistance without it.
findings.truth: Salamis was a major turning point, but Xerxes withdrew with much of his army and Mardonius remained in Greece with a substantial force until Plataea in 479 BC.
findings.evidence: Fetched Wikipedia, Battle of Salamis, aftermath section; Herodotus, Histories 8.68–69 as fetched from the Internet Classics Archive.

findings.claim: Mardonius’ army was doomed without naval supply and Plataea could not have followed Salamis.
findings.truth: Mardonius overwintered in Boeotia and Thessaly, recaptured Athens in 479 BC, and was defeated at Plataea later that year.
findings.evidence: Fetched Wikipedia, Battle of Salamis, aftermath section.

findings.claim: Salamis was decisive in ending the Persian invasion because Plataea could not have followed without it.
findings.truth: Salamis was a major turning point, but Mardonius’s force remained in Greece and was defeated at Plataea in 479 BC.
findings.evidence: Fetched Wikipedia, Battle of Salamis, aftermath section.

findings.claim: Xerxes’ land army was cut off without naval support after Salamis.
findings.truth: Xerxes returned to Asia; Mardonius remained in Greece, and his army was defeated at Plataea in 479 BC.
findings.evidence: Fetched Wikipedia, Battle of Salamis, aftermath section.

findings.truth: The Athenian statesman’s name is Themistocles.
findings.evidence: OCR J199 specification, War and Warfare content; fetched Wikipedia, Battle of Salamis.

summary: Five lessons were checked. Eight surgical edits correct verified factual or specification errors; three broader issues need editorial adjudication.
